title: Göbekli Tepe built
summary: Hunter-gatherers raise massive carved stone pillars arranged in rings on a hilltop — the oldest known monumental architecture, built before farming, pottery or writing.
significance: It overturned the idea that settled farming had to come before monumental religion and building.

title: Jericho's first walls and tower
summary: One of the world's first permanent settlements builds a stone wall and an 8-metre tower, centuries before pottery was known in the region.

title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
summary: People in the hills of the Levant, Anatolia and the Zagros domesticate wheat, barley, lentils, sheep and goats — the start of the Neolithic Revolution.
significance: Agriculture allowed dense populations, cities and states; it arose independently in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and Africa too.

title: Çatalhöyük settled
summary: A huge Neolithic town of mud-brick houses entered through the roofs, with wall paintings and buried ancestors under the floors; it housed several thousand people.

title: Rice farming along the Yangtze
summary: Communities in southern China domesticate rice, while millet is farmed along the Yellow River — East Asia's own agricultural revolution.

title: Maize domesticated in Mexico
summary: Farmers in southern Mexico begin breeding teosinte grass into maize, the crop that would later feed every civilisation of the Americas.

title: Writing invented in Sumer
summary: Temple accountants in Uruk develop cuneiform, pressing wedge-shaped signs into clay tablets — first to count goods, later to record laws, letters and literature.
significance: The beginning of recorded history. Egypt developed hieroglyphs at about the same time; China and Mesoamerica invented writing independently later.

title: Upper and Lower Egypt unified
summary: Kings of Upper Egypt, remembered as Narmer or Menes, unite the Nile Valley and Delta into a single kingdom — the start of pharaonic Egypt.

title: Stonehenge begun
summary: Neolithic Britons dig a circular ditch and bank; over the next thousand years great sarsen and bluestones (some hauled from Wales) are raised into the famous circle.

title: Indus Valley cities flourish
summary: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro grow into planned cities with grid streets, drains, standardized bricks and weights — one of the three great early civilisations alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia.

title: Great Pyramid of Giza completed
summary: Pharaoh Khufu's pyramid, built from about 2.3 million stone blocks, becomes the tallest human-made structure on Earth — a record it held for nearly 4,000 years.

title: Caral, oldest city of the Americas
summary: The Norte Chico civilisation builds platform mounds and sunken plazas at Caral, contemporary with the Egyptian pyramids.

title: Sargon founds the Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian city-states and rules from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean — often called the world's first empire.

title: Epic of Gilgamesh first written
summary: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, are written down; later combined into the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest surviving great work of literature.

title: Minoan palace of Knossos
summary: The Minoans build vast palace complexes on Crete, with frescoes, plumbing and a sea-trading network across the Aegean — Europe's first advanced civilisation.

title: Code of Hammurabi
summary: King Hammurabi of Babylon has 282 laws carved on a basalt stele — 'an eye for an eye' — one of the earliest and most complete written legal codes.

title: Volcanic eruption of Thera
summary: One of the largest eruptions in human history blows apart the island of Thera, burying the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri and sending tsunamis across the Aegean.

title: Shang oracle bones — earliest Chinese writing
summary: Shang dynasty diviners inscribe questions to the ancestors on turtle shells and ox bones; these are the oldest known Chinese characters.

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II clash in perhaps the largest chariot battle ever fought. Both sides claimed victory.
significance: It led to the world's earliest surviving peace treaty, signed about 15 years later.

title: Akhenaten's religious revolution
summary: Pharaoh Akhenaten abandons Egypt's traditional gods for the worship of the sun-disc Aten and builds a new capital at Amarna. His son Tutankhamun restores the old religion.

title: Death of Tutankhamun
summary: The boy-king Tutankhamun dies at about 19. His nearly intact tomb, found in 1922, became the most famous archaeological discovery ever made.

title: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean Greece and cities like Ugarit are destroyed; Egypt barely repels the 'Sea Peoples'. Drought, earthquakes, migration and broken trade all played a part.
significance: A dark age followed; from the ruins emerged iron working, the alphabet-using Phoenicians, Israel and later Classical Greece.

title: Zhou overthrow the Shang
summary: King Wu of Zhou defeats the last Shang king at the Battle of Muye. The Zhou justify it with the 'Mandate of Heaven', an idea that legitimised Chinese dynasties for 3,000 years.

title: Phoenician alphabet spreads
summary: Phoenician traders use a simple 22-letter alphabet; adopted by the Greeks, then the Romans, it is the ancestor of most alphabets used today.

title: Jerusalem becomes Israel's capital
summary: According to the Hebrew Bible, King David makes Jerusalem the capital of a united Israel; his son Solomon builds the First Temple there.

title: Carthage founded
summary: Phoenician settlers from Tyre found Carthage; it becomes the capital of a trading empire spanning the western Mediterranean.

title: First recorded Olympic Games
summary: Greeks from rival city-states gather at Olympia to compete in honour of Zeus. Greek dates were later counted in four-year 'Olympiads' from this year.

title: Legendary founding of Rome
summary: According to legend Romulus founds Rome on the Palatine Hill after killing his twin brother Remus. Archaeology shows villages on the hills around this time.

title: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey
summary: The epic poems of the Trojan War and Odysseus' voyage home are composed around this time, probably from older oral traditions; they become the foundation of Greek education.

title: Assyria destroys the Kingdom of Israel
summary: The Assyrian Empire captures Samaria and deports much of the population of the northern Kingdom of Israel — the origin of the 'ten lost tribes'.

title: Fall of Nineveh
summary: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes sacks Nineveh, capital of the feared Assyrian Empire, which collapses within a few years.

title: Babylon destroys Jerusalem
summary: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys Solomon's Temple and deports Judah's elite to Babylon. The exile shaped Judaism as a religion of scripture.

title: Cyrus the Great takes Babylon
summary: Cyrus of Persia captures Babylon almost without a fight, creating the Achaemenid Empire — the largest the world had yet seen. He lets exiled peoples, including the Jews, return home.

title: The Buddha's enlightenment
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince turned wandering ascetic, attains enlightenment beneath a fig tree and begins teaching the path to end suffering. (His dates are debated by about a century.)

title: Confucius teaches
summary: Kong Fuzi (Confucius) teaches that good government rests on virtue, ritual and respect for family. His ideas shaped Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese society for 2,000 years.

title: Roman Republic founded
summary: Romans expel their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and set up a republic led by two annually elected consuls and the Senate.

title: Democracy in Athens
summary: Cleisthenes reorganises Athens so that all male citizens can vote in the Assembly — the first democracy known to history.

title: Olmec civilisation at San Lorenzo
summary: The Olmec, Mesoamerica's first civilisation, carve colossal stone heads and build ceremonial centres; their calendar, ball game and gods influenced the Maya and Aztecs.

title: The Rigveda composed
summary: Indo-Aryan peoples in north-west India compose the hymns of the Rigveda, the oldest scripture of Hinduism, passed down orally for centuries.

title: Kingdom of Kush rules Egypt
summary: The Nubian kings of Kush, from what is now Sudan, conquer Egypt and rule it as its 25th Dynasty — the 'Black Pharaohs'.

title: First coins struck in Lydia
summary: The kingdom of Lydia mints the first true coins from electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy. Coinage spreads rapidly through the Greek world.

title: Zoroastrianism spreads in Iran
summary: The teachings of the prophet Zarathustra — a cosmic struggle between good and evil — become the faith of the Persian kings. (When he lived is very uncertain.)
